subareas.name: Innovation history / Age of Invention
subareas.coverage: Full: independent sources parallel to (but not duplicating) the subscribed Age of Invention newsletter; invention, productivity and progress with quantitative grounding.

sources.name: Roots of Progress
sources.why: Jason Crawford's series on the history of technology adoption and the drivers of progress — direct systems/constraints angle on invention history.

sources.name: The Puzzle and Its Pieces
sources.why: PEG's series on economic progress, technology adoption and invention ('What Happens in the Gap') — systems angle on why progress happens, complementing Age of Invention without duplicating it.

subareas.name: Quantitative / cliometric history
subareas.coverage: Full: long-run measurement, cycles of history proxied statistically, and historical datasets; the most explicitly 'systems' subarea.

sources.name: Peter Turchin's Substack (Cliodynamics)
sources.why: Quantitative history of empires, cycles and collective action — the canonical cliodynamics voice applying systems theory to history.

sources.name: NBER — Development of the American Economy & Macrohistory
sources.why: Registry of historical macro series (prices, output, factor inputs) and working papers on US long-run economic history — structured data for quantitative history.

sources.name: Economic Growth in History
sources.why: Quantitative economic history on long-run GDP reconstruction, Maddison-dataset discrepancies and growth measurement — cliometric/measurement angle replacing the feed-less Cliodynamics journal.

subareas.name: Logistical & military history (systems view)
subareas.coverage: Implied but core to user's 'logistics' interest; ACOUP is the strongest single source on how supply chains and physical constraints shaped military and political outcomes.

sources.name: Edge Induced Cohesion
sources.why: "A Historian's Eye View of the World" — logistics, feeding armies and material constraints behind campaigns (e.g. white paper on Sherman's Georgia logistics); the strongest ACOUP-parallel for systems military history.

subareas.name: Geography's role in history
subareas.coverage: Full: how terrain, water, climate and resource endowments shaped development paths — a central stated interest.

sources.name: From Poverty to Progress
sources.why: Stefen Klein's multi-series economic history covering 'why some nations became rich' with explicit geography, soils and tsetse-fly/cattle crop-yield causal analysis.

sources.name: Sam Matey-Coste (China's Hydrological History)
sources.why: Geography-driven history of water systems, flood control and canal infrastructure shaping China's state and economy — physical-constraints history.

subareas.name: History of economics & economic thought
subareas.coverage: Full: the intellectual and measurement history of economics itself, plus long-run economic history research.

sources.name: Davis Kedrosky — Economic History journal blog
sources.why: Series on 'The History of Economic History' tracing how fields and their quantitative methods evolved — meta-history of economics.

subareas.name: History of politics, institutions & political economy
subareas.coverage: Full: how institutions, incentives and market structure (systems) shaped political-economic outcomes over time.

sources.name: The Diff
sources.why: Byrne Hobart's systems take on how financial and industrial structure evolved historically — institutions and incentives applied to market history.

sources.name: Free Markets & Firepower
sources.why: Economic and political history linking fiscal/monetary systems ('price of time') to state power — history of politics and economics through incentives.

sources.name: Marginal Revolution
sources.why: Market/economic-history commentary with heavy systems, incentives and constraining-geography content; complements the Diff for political economy.

subareas.name: Long-run data, technology adoption & material constraints
subareas.coverage: Full: empirical long-run series on growth, energy, technology diffusion and physical limits.

sources.name: Our World in Data — Technology & Growth long-run series
sources.why: Registry of long-run historical series (technology adoption, energy, GDP per capita) with systems-oriented writeups — complements NBER and OWID's own feeds.

subareas.name: Geography / systems-resilience (broad context)
subareas.coverage: Partial/implied — one cross-cutting source bridging geography, shipping chokepoints and system fragility.

sources.name: The Great Simplification (systems-history episodes)
sources.why: Systems economist Nate Hagens interviews historians on chokepoints, shipping and material constraints shaping civilization — geography-systems angle.

registries.name: Our World in Data — long-run historical indicators
OpenAlex API (journal/work discovery for Cliodynamics & economic history)
EH.net (Economic History Association) data & book-abstract archive

news_vs_analysis.description: Mix skews heavily to analysis/first-principles (blogs, newsletters, academic method) rather than hard news — appropriate for a systems-history topic where events are historical and the value is causal reconstruction. 'News'-like sources are limited to working-paper/feed announcements (NBER, Economic History Review) and periodic long-run data updates (Our World in Data).

notes: Boundary check: excluded narrative/political history without systems content (e.g., pure biography channels, local nostalgia blogs) and confirmed all sources carry an explicit systems/constraints/logistics/quantitative angle. Subscribed/blacklisted domains respected: antonhowes.substack.com, livinglondonhistory.com, spitalfieldslife.com are excluded and no domain in this list duplicates them. Source-type mix: independent blog (ACOUP, Roots of Progress, Marginal Revolution, Works in Progress), newsletter/Substack (From Poverty to Progress, Sam Matey-Coste, Turchin, Free Markets & Firepower, The Diff), academic/journal (Cliodynamics, Economic History Review), data/registry (NBER, Our World in Data, EH.net), podcast (The Great Simplification) - >=4 distinct types satisfied. Feed-verified (check_url ok): acoup.blog, frompovertytoprogress, sammatey, peterturchin, blog.daviskedrosky, ourworldindata, marginalrevolution, thediff, worksinprogress, rootsofprogress, freemarketsandfirepower, nber, academic.oup.com, api.openalex.org. Deprioritized (stale/no feed) after probing: rulesofthegame.blog (feed stale 2022), eh.net listed only as a registry crawl since its feed is stale, globalmacrodata.com (feed blocked). thegreatsimplification.com was surfaced by web_search but not independently feed-verified (search budget exhausted) - marked medium confidence with a crawl_root to re-probe at L1. Academic/paywalled endpoints directed to RSS/API: Cliodynamics via OpenAlex (api.openalex.org), Economic History Review via OUP RSS.
